questions.q: What does "accuracy" mean in the context of media ethics?
questions.a: Accuracy means reporting facts correctly and verifying information with reliable sources before publishing it. A wrong answer suggests the student confuses "accuracy" with "speed" or "popularity," missing the core requirement of truth-telling.

questions.q: Why is "independence" an important ethical principle for the media?
questions.a: Independence ensures that news is not influenced by advertisers, politicians, or powerful people who might want to hide the truth. If a student thinks independence means "the media can say anything," they misunderstand that it actually means "the media cannot be bought or controlled."

questions.q: If a newspaper only interviews the winning team of a match and ignores the losing team, which ethical principle have they violated?
questions.a: They have violated "fairness" and "objectivity." To fix this, they should include the perspectives of both teams. A wrong answer suggests the student doesn't understand that ethical journalism requires presenting multiple sides of a story.

questions.q: Why is it ethically wrong for a reporter to share the private home address of a crime victim?
questions.a: It violates the principle of "privacy," which mandates that the media must protect the dignity and safety of individuals, especially victims. If the answer focuses on "law," the student is straying outside the scope of ethics into legal territory.

questions.q: Should a newspaper accept money from a political party to write only good things about them? Why or why not?
questions.a: No, because it violates "independence." Taking money creates a conflict of interest, making the reporting biased rather than objective. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks journalism is a business first rather than a public service.

questions.q: Create a checklist a reporter should use before posting a news story on social media.
questions.a: The checklist should include: 1) Are these facts verified? 2) Have I heard from both sides? 3) Am I being pressured by anyone? 4) Am I respecting the privacy of the people in the story? Poor answers will lack these specific ethical pillars.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Media ethics are the set of moral rules that guide journalists to report the truth accurately, fairly, and ______.
Fill in the blank: Have you ever seen two ______ tell the same story differently?
What is Media ethics? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Media ethics are the set of moral rules that guide journalists to report the truth accurately, fairly, and independently.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Media ethics?
questions.a: Students often believe "media" is the same as "opinion." They assume that because a person is on TV or writing a blog, everything they say is a "fact." They fail to distinguish between objective reporting (facts) and subjective commentary (personal views).

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to identify whether a news report follows ethical standards (accuracy, objectivity, fairness, independence, and privacy) by analyzing a provided news snippet.
